issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette:
# Marcus

Marcus was forty-nine when it happened. He had been driving the 42 line—a cross-town route through the city's west side—for nearly fifteen years, a job he had come to love for its solitude and rhythm, the way the familiar streets and faces of regular passengers had woven themselves into the fabric of his days. On a Tuesday evening in late October, during the final run before the night shift took over, two men boarded near the industrial park. Marcus remembers the sound of their voices—low, coordinated, the way they moved toward him with a purpose that felt different from the usual press of commuters. One pulled a knife. The assault happened in the vehicle's back compartment, in the dark, in a space Marcus had always thought of as his own. What stayed with him most vividly was not the pain but the absolute helplessness—the way his body had betrayed him, the way he had been unmade in a place where he had always felt safe.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus told no one. He took two weeks off, told his wife Angela that he had the flu, and spent those days in a fog of shame so thick he could barely move. He had come to believe that what had happened to his body—the violation, the loss of control—was somehow a mark on him that others could see, a sign of weakness or complicity that made him less of a man. When he returned to driving, he was different. The 42 line, which had once been his refuge, had become a minefield. Fatigue had begun to creep into his days—a bone-deep exhaustion that was partly insomnia, partly the weight of dread—and on mornings when he felt particularly tired or worn down, the thought of getting behind the wheel filled him with a formless terror. He was certain now that people couldn't be trusted, that the world was fundamentally unsafe, and that his own body had proven itself unreliable. These convictions arrived not as abstract thoughts but as bodily certainties, settling into his chest like stones.

The connections between his exhaustion and what came next formed quickly. When Marcus felt very tired—which was most days now—something in him would shift. The fatigue seemed to open a door in his mind, and through it would pour the memory itself: the sound of their voices, the smell of the vehicle's interior, the sensation of being pinned. The memory came not as a distant recollection but as a present-tense replay, a film looping without mercy, and each time it played, the terror returned with it, as raw as the night itself. The shame returned too, a burning across his face and through his body. These memories, once triggered by his exhaustion, would then reshape how he saw the world. Each replay reinforced his conviction that people were predatory, that trust was naive, that his body was a source of shame rather than home. And that mistrust, that loss of faith in the basic safety of human connection, would in turn make him hypervigilant to new triggers. When a passenger sat too close, when someone's tone sounded off, when the bus grew quiet in a way that felt loaded—these ordinary moments would activate his sense of danger, which would pull the memory forward again, which would flood him with terror and shame. Each of these triggers arrived with a thought so immediate it felt like fact: that people were predatory, that the world had shown him its true nature, that his body was a liability. The passenger sitting too close wasn't just a sensory event—it was proof that he couldn't protect himself, that trust was a fool's errand.

Driving with others became increasingly difficult. What had once been the ordinary texture of his job—the presence of passengers, the conversations, the casual intimacy of shared space—now felt like a constant threat. Every time he saw passengers boarding, or heard voices rising from the back of the bus, the thought arrived with the same weight as memory: this is where it happened, and it could happen again. The sight of two men together made him certain, with a logic he couldn't argue with, that he would never be safe in this space. He began requesting the quieter routes, the off-peak hours, anything to minimize the number of people on the bus. But even empty buses triggered him; the silence itself carried menace. Four months after the assault, Angela found him in the garage one evening, gripping the steering wheel of their car, unable to drive home from a depot meeting because there were other drivers present. He had sat there for forty minutes, waiting for everyone else to leave, his hands shaking. She asked him what was wrong. He couldn't tell her. The shame of it—of being afraid, of being broken, of what had been done to him—felt like it would destroy everything if he spoke it aloud.

By the time Marcus came to the clinic, he had been on medical leave for six weeks. His PCL-5 score was 76. He moved through the intake with a kind of numb compliance, answering questions but offering little. What he wanted most, he said quietly, was to understand why his mind kept replaying what had happened, why he couldn't seem to trust anyone anymore, and whether he would ever be able to drive again without feeling like he was about to shatter.
